chapter_theme: The second quarter of Agappei Siddhar's songs widens the negation from the paths to the practices and the practitioner: yoga does not free, however long it is held; sastras and sutras are mere imagining; wandering to the sky brings rebirth; and the deeds one has done do not leave. Against this the stanzas set one instruction, repeated as a refrain within the refrain, சும்மா இரு, just be still, and a few bare statements: the Lord is bliss, Saivam is what stands by itself, where desire has ended there is right conduct, and the Lord is like fire and like the pillar, neither male nor female. Sun and moon, nectar and poison, and the letters அ and உ as anava and its bent companion show the poet still speaking the Siddhars' cipher while telling the demon to stop.
structure_note: 1667 to 1669 deny yoga and define the Lord as bliss; 1670 to 1674 are a dialogue in which the demon claims to have seen and is told that seeing by another's word is desire, that karma stays, and that sastras are imagining; 1675 to 1678 ask about karma, yoga and shame; 1679 gives the instruction to be still, which 1686 and 1690 repeat; 1680 to 1683 are reproaches and the definition of Saivam; 1684 to 1689 return to the cipher (letters, nothingness, sun and moon, the fire that is neither male nor female); 1690 and 1691 close against study and against forest tapas.

1667.reading: Yoga will not do, demon; when you have seen what is, knowledge is the body itself, and I have told you not to go seeking.
1667.nuance: தேக ஞானம் may mean knowledge of the body, knowledge that the body is (the body as cosmos), or knowledge while embodied. The denial of yoga continues the ladder begun in 1666 and is pressed again in 1676.

1668.reading: It is a five-headed serpent, demon, and the gain from it is small; our Lord, you have seen, is the one who cures this poison.
1668.nuance: The five-headed serpent is read by tradition either as the five senses, whose poison is desire, or as the coiled power with its five faces; ஆதாயம் கொஞ்சம் (little profit) fits the senses better. The Lord as antidote (விடந்தீர்க்கும்) recalls the Siva who drank poison, and 1642's warning against poison.

1669.reading: All that is called 'Lord', demon, of what kind is it? Hear me tell you: it is bliss.
1669.nuance: The poet's one positive definition of the Lord in the work: not a form, a letter or a place, but ஆனந்தம். It answers 1660, which said what the Lord is not.

1670.reading: 'I have found it, I have opened my love, I have taken it in,' says the demon; 'you have told me what is.'
1670.nuance: The stanza reads as the demon's reply, since the refrain address sits inside what sounds like a claim of attainment and the last line is in the second person (சொன்னாயே, you told). 1671 to 1673 are the poet's answer, denying that a told truth is one's own.

1671.reading: Even when what is has been told, demon, you must see it by yourself; the deceit will not end, and for those who merely saw it is desire.
1671.nuance: A rebuke to second-hand knowledge: hearing the truth leaves கள்ளம் (deceit, the hidden self-regard) intact, and even seeing without becoming is a form of காமம், wanting. The point is pressed on the poet's own words too.

1672.reading: Even those who stand knowing, demon, do not fear, I tell you; the strong deeds you have done will not leave you.
1672.nuance: அஞ்சார்கள் can be praise (the knowers are fearless) or blame (they do not fear karma as they should); the second line, that one's done deeds do not depart, suits the warning. The stanza admits what little else in the work does, that karma is not dissolved by knowing.

1673.reading: It is the Lord's bond, demon; all that you have seen in this way is bond practised; you have seen the Supreme.
1673.nuance: ஈசன் பாசம் may mean the bond that the Lord lays (the Siddhanta view that pasam is his instrument) or bondage to the Lord as one more attachment. பாசம் பயின்றது, bond practised or habituated, treats all seeing as bondage, and the last line either exempts the Supreme or ironically includes it.

1674.reading: Sastras and sutras, demon, and all that is imagining: they must not be looked at; you have seen their fruit, the void.
1674.nuance: சங்கற்பம் is the mind's resolve or construction; scripture and aphorism are placed under it. பாழ் பலம் is barren fruit, and 1692 and 1708 give பாழ் a second, positive sense as the emptiness beside the Supreme.

1675.reading: Have you seen the way, demon, for that karma to end? To clear and grow clear, bathe in the holy water too.
1675.nuance: The stanza can be read straight, as a rare endorsement of bathing at a tirtha, or as irony against those who think a bath clears karma, in line with the work's rejection of rites. The inner tirtha of the yogis is a third reading; the stanza does not decide.

1676.reading: However long you hold to yoga, demon, what of it? Will you become one who is freed, and will there be release?
1676.nuance: The two questions expect the answer no; முத்தன் (the freed one) and மோட்சம் are both denied to yoga held for any length of time. This is the sharpest of the stanzas against yoga, and sits oddly with the breath lore in 1688 and 1702.

1677.reading: Do not seek your own destruction, demon, I tell you; even when the bond has gone, the souls do not go.
1677.nuance: பசுக்கள் (souls, in the Siddhanta sense of pasu) remain even when paasam is removed: the stanza may be stating the doctrine that the soul is eternal and is not destroyed in release, or warning that the self (the demon) persists after its bonds loosen. நாசம் ஆவதற்கே நாடாதே forbids seeking annihilation.

1678.reading: What is shame for, demon, once good deeds have ended? If you want to see it, it cannot be seen.
1678.nuance: நல்வினை தீர்ந்தக்கால் may mean the exhaustion of good karma along with bad, after which shame has no object; or that when one has stopped doing even good works there is nothing to be ashamed of. The last line denies that the real can be an object of seeing.

1679.reading: Just be still, demon; I have told you the formula. The place where you stayed still is what was pointed to.
1679.nuance: சும்மா இரு (simply be, do nothing) is the work's one positive instruction, called a சூத்திரம் in mockery of the sutras rejected in 1674. சுட்டது is from சுட்டு (to point out) or சுடு (to burn); the stillness is either the thing indicated or the thing that burns away the rest. 1686 and 1690 repeat it.

1680.reading: Without seeing yourself, demon, you entered into flesh; without seeing me, you came to this place.
1680.nuance: Who speaks as 'me' is unclear: the self addressing the mind, the guru, or the Lord. On any reading, embodiment is traced to a failure of seeing, and the mind's arrival in the body is a mistake it can undo by seeing.

1681.reading: Even if you run to the sky, demon, you will come back and be born; without eating the honey you have roamed the streets.
1681.nuance: The sky-run is the yogi's ascent (to the crown, or to the heavens); the stanza says even that returns to birth. தேன் (honey) is the nectar within, which the Siddhars say is nearer than any journey; the street-roaming is the seeker's wandering, condemned again in 1698.

1682.reading: Saivam, demon, is what stands as itself; if there is no Saivam, trouble comes, you have seen.
1682.nuance: தானாய் நின்றது, standing as itself, defines Saivam as a state rather than a sect; 1695 and 1696 define it as the place where self has gone and as self-knowledge. சலம் is agitation or the flux that comes without it.

1683.reading: Where desire has ended, demon, you have seen right conduct; wherever you go, there is the Lord's bond.
1683.nuance: ஆசாரம், the rules of conduct that the poet otherwise disdains, is redefined as desirelessness itself. The second line repeats 1673 and can be read as a consolation (the Lord's hold is everywhere) or a warning (bondage follows wherever one goes).

1684.reading: Anava is the root, demon, and it came as the letter அ; the crooked letter உ was born along with it.
1684.nuance: A second reading of Om's letters after 1655 and 1656: there அ was the first arising and ம was maya; here அ is ஆணவம், the root impurity of self-regard, and கோணும் உகாரம் (the bent உ) its companion. The two schemes are not reconciled; tradition reads them as keys to different levels.

1685.reading: There is nothing at all, demon; it has come to be just as it is; there is no good, no evil, and no shame.
1685.nuance: ஒன்றும் இல்லை and உள்ளபடி ஆச்சு sit side by side: nothing is, and what is is as it is. The denial of good and evil is the stance of the one beyond the pairs, as 1709 and 1711 extend it to caste, self and Lord.

1686.reading: The place where you stayed still, demon, is what was pointed to, I have told you; I do not know what maya this is, and I do not see even myself.
1686.nuance: The repetition of 1679's second half is followed by a confession: the poet does not know what the appearance is and cannot see himself. Not seeing oneself (என்னையும் காணேன்) may be failure or the goal, since 1711 denies the self altogether.

1687.reading: What are the arts for, demon? Will not those who see laugh? What are the stages for? Who are you? Tell me.
1687.nuance: கலைகள் are the sastras or arts and நிலைகள் the graded states of practice; both are mocked. நீயார் (who are you) is the one question the work keeps asking the demon, and 1665 promised the way to answer it.

1688.reading: The moon is nectar, demon, and the sun is poison; the moon is white and the sun is red.
1688.nuance: In the Siddhars' cipher the moon and sun are the left and right breaths, or the crown and the lower fire; the moon's nectar and the sun's poison (that dries the nectar) are Tirumanthiram doctrine. The colours match the two mandalas. The stanza states the cipher without applying it, and 1702 then says that even riding the breath does not bring the Lord.

1689.reading: Not male and not female, demon: you have seen the fire; the pillar is likewise, and so is the sadguru, you have seen.
1689.nuance: அக்கினி (fire) and தாணு (the pillar, Siva as sthanu, the fixed one) are given as images of what has no sex; the guru is placed with them. Fire as the Lord's likeness recalls the linga of flame; the stanza says nothing of Siva's male and female halves.

1690.reading: Whatever you study, demon, it will not be our word; you have heard what was said: just be still.
1690.nuance: எம்முரை (our word) sets the guru's spoken teaching against books. The instruction of 1679 returns as the conclusion of all the saying: the demon has heard, and the rest is stillness.

1691.reading: Forest and hill, demon: what if one does hard tapas there? Will release be laid open? Is it not the truth that is needed?
1691.nuance: The stanza puts the standard Siddhar case against ascetic retreat: place and severity do not open வீடு; மெய் (truth, or the real) does. 1697 and 1720 continue it against renunciants and beggars.

links.note: Sivavakkiyar says that in clear yoga one reaches sarupam, the Lord's form; Agappei asks what use yoga held for any length of time is and whether it yields release, expecting no. The conflict holds if sarupam counts as release; it eases if Agappei, like Tirumular in 2525, treats sarupam as a graded state short of it.

Tirumular makes the stillness in which there is no moving (அசைவு இல்லாமை) the mark of sanmarga; Agappei's one formula is சும்மா இரு, be still, and the place where one stays still is the thing pointed to. Both end the path in motionlessness, though Tirumular reaches it through removing pasu and pasam and Agappei by stopping.

Tirumular says that when bindu and nada meet the moon, nectar wells up in the inner sky; Agappei states the key, the moon is nectar and white, the sun poison and red. The same cipher of the inner moon as nectar is used, but Agappei only names it and in 1702 denies that working the breath brings the Lord.

Tirumular asks whether wasting oneself away is tapas; Agappei asks what hard tapas in forest and hill achieves and whether it opens release. Both deny that severity of place and body is the way, and both put something inward (the Siva-state, the truth) in its stead.

Sivavakkiyar asks whether those who leave their land to clear forest, hill and hollow will see the Lord's feet and says none of them has gained release; Agappei asks what hard tapas in forest and hill will give and whether release is laid open by it. The two Siddhars make the same case against ascetic wandering.

source_issues: 1670: the stanza appears to be spoken by the demon (last line சொன்னாயே, second person), not by the poet; the printed text gives no speaker marks.
1679 and 1686 line 2 and 4 சுட்டது can be from சுட்டு (point out) or சுடு (burn); the spelling does not decide it.
